Market Auction Mechanics – Passive vs. Aggressive Participants market structure analysis

Every market transaction requires one passive participant (limit order) and one aggressive participant (market order). Passive buyers place bids on the order book; passive sellers place offers. Aggressive buyers buy on the ask; aggressive sellers sell on the bid. A transaction completes only when a market order hits a limit order. Price moves up when aggressive buyers exhaust all passive sellers on the ask at a given level; price moves down when aggressive sellers exhaust all passive buyers on the bid. The number of aggressive participants relative to passive orders determines direction—not whether there are more buyers than sellers, since every completed transaction pairs exactly one buyer with one seller. Understanding this auction framework is the foundation of all order flow analysis, applicable to any instrument or strategy.

Best entry for Range Trap — Sweep Both Sides of a Defined Range setup

The range trap setup exploits the predictable accumulation of stop losses and pending orders at both extremes of a consolidating range. The trap setup uses this structure as follows: (1) Mark the range high and range low clearly; (2) Wait for price to sweep one side — e.g., sweep below the range low to trigger sell stops; (3) Watch for an immediate reversal back inside the range — this confirms the sweep was a trap rather than a breakdown; (4) Enter in the direction of the reversal (long if the low was swept, short if the high was swept); (5) Stop loss is placed just beyond the swept extreme; (6) Target is the opposite side of the range — the opposing liquidity pool. The range trap is especially reliable when price has tested a range extreme multiple times without a clean breakdown, as each test accumulates more stop orders at that level. When the sweep finally fires, the volume of trapped participants fueling the reversal is proportionally larger.

Best practices for Candlestick Psychology — Momentum, Long Wick, Indecision

Each candlestick can be classified by the relationship between its body size and wick size, revealing the balance of power between buyers and sellers. A momentum candle has a large body with small wicks — one side dominated nearly the entire period, indicating strong directional pressure likely to continue. A long-wicked candle has a small body with a long wick in one direction — the losing side (bears for a bottom wick, bulls for a top wick) made a significant push but was reversed near the close, known as the 'comeback kid' pattern, signaling a potential reversal. An indecision candle (doji) has equal-sized wicks with a small body, showing neither side won — neither a bullish nor bearish signal. All three candle types are only meaningful at swing highs, swing lows, or at the end of pullbacks; candles forming in random mid-trend positions carry no interpretive value.
